sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

sources.text:
**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

> Source: Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar (Venomous animal accidents: what to do and how to avoid them). https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

validation_inputs.draft:
**Do not walk.** Have your friends carry you on a stretcher, chair, or back-to-back immediately.

Walking accelerates venom effects and delays critical care [S1], [S2].

**Immediate Action Steps:**
1.  **Stop moving:** Get away from the snake immediately [S1].
2.  **Rest the limb:** Keep your leg and the whole body still while waiting for transport [S1], [S2].
3.  **Remove tight items:** Take off rings, bracelets, shoes, or socks before swelling starts [S1], [S6].
4.  **Arrange transport:** Have helpers carry you rather than walking; do not attempt to walk a mile to the road [S1], [S2].
5.  **Seek medical care urgently:** Antivenom is the only effective treatment; home remedies or waiting will not fix envenoming [S6].

**What NOT to do:**
*   Do **not** use a tight arterial tourniquet [S1], [S2], [S6].
*   Do **not** cut, suck, burn, or apply herbs/liquids to the bite [S6].
*   Do **not** try to catch or kill the snake (risk of re-bite); a photo from a distance is safer if needed for identification [S5], [S6].

**Warning:** Snakebite outcomes depend on the snake type, venom amount, and time to treatment. Delaying transport by walking increases the risk of severe tissue damage or systemic failure [S4]. Call emergency services immediately while being carried.

The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

validation_inputs.draft:
**NO.** Do **not** tie a tight band or use a tourniquet above the bite. This can cause severe tissue damage and is not recommended for an unidentified snake [S1], [S2], [S6].

### Immediate Steps to Take:

1.  **Get Away:** Immediately move away from the immediate danger area to avoid re-biting [S1], [S6].
2.  **Keep Still:** Keep the person and the bitten limb completely still [S1], [S2], [S6]. Movement accelerates venom spread.
3.  **Remove Constrictions:** Remove tight items like rings, bracelets, or shoes from the bitten area before swelling occurs [S1], [S6].
4.  **Arrange Transport:** Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher; do not make them walk [S1], [S2].
5.  **Monitor Breathing:** Monitor breathing while waiting for help [S1], [S2].
6.  **Clean if Possible (Context Dependent):**
    *   If in Brazil or following American Medical Association/Red Cross guidance: Wash the area with soap and water [S3], [S6].
    *   Note: Australian guidelines advise against cleaning the wound to preserve venom traces for identification kits [S3].
7.  **Offer Water:** If the person is conscious, offer water [S6].

### What NOT To Do:
*   **Do not** apply a tight arterial tourniquet [S1], [S2], [S6].
*   **Do not** use unproven traditional remedies, cut the wound, suck the venom, burn the area, or apply substances like herbs, kerosene, alcohol, or coffee grounds [S2], [S6].
*   **Do not** try to catch or kill the snake; this risks re-envenomation or a second bite [S5].

### Important Safety Note:
*   **Pressure-immobilization bandaging** is **not** universal. The World Health Organization limits its use specifically to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Since you do not know the snake species, do not apply this technique [S1], [S2], [S3].
*   **Antivenom** is the only effective treatment for envenoming; first aid is only a bridge to urgent care [S6].

***Not backed by local sources:** The outcome of a snakebite depends on multiple factors including the snake's species, size, venom amount, and the bite location. Even a "minor" bite can be fatal in certain circumstances (e.g., face or abdomen), while others may cause only moderate injury [S4]. Access to effective treatment is a major challenge in many regions, so rapid transport is critical [S4].

**Warning:** This information is for emergency first aid only. It does not replace professional medical advice. Seek immediate help from a doctor or health facility.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

validation_inputs.draft:
**Do not walk.** You should have people carry you on a stretcher or be carried by helpers.

*   **Reason:** Walking accelerates venom effects. The WHO specifically states: "Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects." [S1]
*   **Action:** Instruct your friend to arrange for you to be carried immediately to the nearest health facility.

**Additional Immediate Steps:**
1.  **Get away from danger:** Move away from the snake's location immediately. [S1]
2.  **Keep still:** Keep yourself and the bitten leg as still as possible while being transported. [S1]
3.  **Remove tight items:** Remove rings, bracelets, shoes, or tight clothing near the bite site before swelling starts. [S1], [S6]
4.  **Monitor breathing:** Watch for breathing difficulties while waiting for transport. [S1], [S2]

**DO NOT DO THE FOLLOWING:**
*   Do **not** use a tight arterial tourniquet or tight bandage unless specifically trained and guided for neurotoxic bites (generally avoid if unsure). [S1]
*   Do **not** cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, or coffee grounds. [S6]
*   Do **not** try to catch or kill the snake; this risks a second bite. [S5], [S6]

**Warning Signs & Professional Help:**
Snakebites are medical emergencies requiring urgent antivenom treatment. [S6]. Seek professional help immediately; this first aid does not replace a doctor. If you experience difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or severe weakness, these are critical warning signs.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

3.  **Remove tight items** (rings, bracelets, shoes) near the bite site before swelling occurs [S1][S6].
4.  **Arrange urgent transport** to a hospital immediately; have helpers carry the person rather than making them walk [S1][S2].
5.  **Wash the area with soap and water** if available [S3][S6].
6.  **Monitor breathing** while waiting for help [S1][S2].

**Why no tight band?**
*   WHO guidelines explicitly state: "Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet" [S1][S2].
*   Pressure-immobilization is not universal; it is limited to specific neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling and should not be used for unidentified snakes [S1][S2].
*   Using a tight band on an unknown bite may increase tissue damage if the venom causes local destruction [S3].

**Important Notes:**
*   **Antivenom is the only effective treatment** for envenoming; first aid is temporary until professional care is reached [S6].
*   Do not attempt to catch or kill the snake, as this risks re-envenomation [S5].
*   If possible, take a photo of the snake from a safe distance to assist identification, but do not delay transport [S6].

**Warning:** Snakebite outcomes depend on the snake type, bite location, victim's health, and time to treatment. Some bites can be fatal even if they seem minor initially [S4]. **This information does not replace professional medical advice.** Seek emergency care immediately.

sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

request.q: A snake bit my leg. My friend can call for transport. Should I walk a mile to the road or have people carry me?

results.answer:
**Local passages supplied.** They may not support every part of this answer; citations are not independently verified.

**Do not walk.** Have your friend arrange for you to be carried on a stretcher or by helpers immediately [1], [2].

**Step-by-Step Action Plan:**

1.  **Stop Moving Immediately:** Sit or lie down right where you are. Do not try to walk a mile to the road, as walking accelerates venom effects and can make the bite life-threatening [1].
2.  **Get Help with Transport:** Ask your friend to organize for people to carry you on a stretcher to the nearest health facility or road where an ambulance is available [1], [2].
3.  **Keep Still:** Once safe, keep both yourself and the bitten leg completely still until medical help arrives [1], [2].
4.  **Remove Tight Items:** Have helpers remove rings, bracelets, watches, or tight shoes from the affected limb before swelling occurs [1], [6].
5.  **Monitor Breathing:** Watch for signs of breathing difficulty while waiting for transport [1], [2].

**What NOT to do:**
*   Do not try to catch or kill the snake (this puts rescuers at risk and wastes time) [5].
*   Do not apply tourniquets, cut the wound, suck the venom, or apply herbs/substances [1], [6].

**When to Seek Professional Help:**
This is a medical emergency. Antivenom is the only effective treatment for envenoming, and outcomes depend heavily on how quickly you reach a facility with it [4], [6]. Even if symptoms seem mild initially, venom can cause severe systemic effects or death [3], [4]. Go to the hospital immediately.

*Disclaimer: This information is for emergency first aid only and does not replace professional medical advice.*

> ⚠️ First-aid guidance only; it does not replace medical care. If help is available, seek it.

Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

**Do not walk.** Have your friend arrange for you to be carried on a stretcher or by helpers immediately [S1], [S2].

**Step-by-Step Action Plan:**

1.  **Stop Moving Immediately:** Sit or lie down right where you are. Do not try to walk a mile to the road, as walking accelerates venom effects and can make the bite life-threatening [S1].
2.  **Get Help with Transport:** Ask your friend to organize for people to carry you on a stretcher to the nearest health facility or road where an ambulance is available [S1], [S2].
3.  **Keep Still:** Once safe, keep both yourself and the bitten leg completely still until medical help arrives [S1], [S2].
4.  **Remove Tight Items:** Have helpers remove rings, bracelets, watches, or tight shoes from the affected limb before swelling occurs [S1], [S6].
5.  **Monitor Breathing:** Watch for signs of breathing difficulty while waiting for transport [S1], [S2].

**What NOT to do:**
*   Do not try to catch or kill the snake (this puts rescuers at risk and wastes time) [S5].
*   Do not apply tourniquets, cut the wound, suck the venom, or apply herbs/substances [S1], [S6].

**When to Seek Professional Help:**
This is a medical emergency. Antivenom is the only effective treatment for envenoming, and outcomes depend heavily on how quickly you reach a facility with it [S4], [S6]. Even if symptoms seem mild initially, venom can cause severe systemic effects or death [S3], [S4]. Go to the hospital immediately.

*Disclaimer: This information is for emergency first aid only and does not replace professional medical advice.*

sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

No. Do **not** tie a tight band or use an arterial tourniquet on an unidentified snakebite. This can worsen tissue damage and is not recommended when the venom type is unknown.

Steps:
1. Move away from the snake if safe.
2. Keep the person calm, lying down, and still; do not let them walk [S1].
3. Remove tight items (rings, bracelets, shoes) from the bitten limb before swelling starts [S6].
4. If conscious and able to swallow safely, offer water [S6].
5. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility; have helpers carry the person on a stretcher rather than walking [S1][S2].
6. Monitor breathing while help is obtained [S1][S2].

Not backed by local sources:
- Washing the bite with soap and water is recommended by some organizations (e.g., American Medical Association, American Red Cross), but Australian guidelines advise against cleaning the wound; do this only if it does not delay transport or remove venom traces needed for identification [S3].
- Do not attempt to catch, kill, or identify the snake; this risks re-envenomation or a second bite. A photo from a distance may help identification later [S5].

Warning signs requiring immediate professional help:
- Difficulty breathing, drooling, swelling of the face/tongue, severe pain spreading quickly, numbness, weakness, confusion, or bleeding under the skin.

Seek professional medical care immediately; antivenom is the only effective treatment for envenoming [S6]. This information does not replace a doctor's advice.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

validation_inputs.draft:
**NÃO.** Você **não deve** aplicar um torniquete ou garrote acima da picada.

Aqui estão os motivos e o procedimento correto:

### Por que NÃO usar torniquete
*   **Ineficácia e Perigo:** Torniquetes não são eficazes contra a maioria dos venenos de cobra e podem cortar a circulação sanguínea, levando à gangrena ou amputação do membro. [S5]
*   **Risco de Lesão Grave:** A restrição severa da circulação pode causar danos permanentes ao tecido, piores do que a picada em si se não houver tratamento imediato. [S5]
*   **Recomendação Oficial:** O Ministério da Saúde e a Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS) alertam explicitamente contra o uso de torniquete arterial apertado. [S1][S2]

### O que FAZER (Passos Imediatos)
1.  **Afaste-se da cobra:** Não tente capturá-la. Tire uma foto à distância se possível para identificação futura. [S1]
2.  **Mantenha a vítima calma e imóvel:** Deite-a imediatamente. Mantenha o membro picado em repouso absoluto (sem movimentar) para retardar a disseminação do veneno pelo sistema linfático. [S1][S2]
3.  **Remova objetos apertados:** Tire anéis, pulseiras e calçados logo de início, pois o membro pode inchar rapidamente. [S1]
4.  **Lave o local:** Lave a picada com água e sabão para reduzir bactérias superficiais. [S1][S3] *(Nota: A OMS sugere cautela se houver risco de usar traços de veneno na pele para identificação, mas a limpeza geral é padrão em muitas guias locais como a do Brasil).*
5.  **Transporte URGENTE:** Leve a vítima imediatamente a um hospital de referência. O soro antiveneno é o único tratamento eficaz conhecido. [S1]
    *   Se não houver ambulância, peça ajuda para transportar a pessoa em uma maca; evite fazê-la caminhar. [S2]
6.  **Hidratação:** Ofereça água apenas se a vítima estiver consciente e capaz de engolir com segurança. [S1]

### O que NÃO FAZER (Erros Comuns)
*   Não faça cortes na picada. [S5]
*   Não tente sugar o veneno (com boca ou bomba). [S5]
*   Não aplique gelo, fogo, álcool, pó de café, querosene ou ervas no local. [S1][S5]
*   Não dê bebidas alcoólicas. [S1]

> **Atenção:** A eficácia de bandagens compressivas varia conforme o tipo de cobra e a região; sem saber a espécie, a regra geral segura é manter o membro imóvel sem amarrar nada. O foco principal deve ser o transporte rápido para atendimento médico especializado. [S3]

A bandagem compressiva depende do veneno e da orientação local; cobra ou local desconhecido não permite concluir que seja adequada. Observe a respiração enquanto busca ajuda.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

English editorial summary by Emergency AI, checked 2026-11-26; not a publisher translation, complete manual or clinical certification. Attribution does not imply publisher endorsement.

request.q: Me mordió una serpiente de especie desconocida. ¿Debo apretar una banda por encima de la mordedura?

results.answer:
**Fragmentos locales proporcionados.** Puede que no respalden toda la respuesta; las citas no se han verificado de forma independiente.

**Respuesta generada retenida.** Falló una comprobación de citas o de las condiciones de una acción. Consulte las referencias originales a continuación y busque ayuda cualificada. Estas comprobaciones no garantizan la exactitud médica ni verifican todas las afirmaciones.



**Orientación alternativa basada en fuentes**

La respuesta generada no está disponible. Estos pasos proceden de las referencias versionadas que aparecen abajo; respete sus condiciones.

Ante una posible mordedura de serpiente, mantenga a la persona y el miembro mordido inmóviles y organice traslado urgente a atención médica [2]. Pida que ayudantes lleven a la persona en una camilla hasta el transporte en vez de hacerla caminar [2]. No use un torniquete arterial apretado ni remedios tradicionales sin eficacia demostrada [2]. sources.doc_title: Primeros auxilios y cuidados de salud
sources.text:
**Haga:**
- Aléjese de la serpiente; no intente capturarla (una foto a distancia ayuda a identificarla).
- Mantenga a la víctima **tranquila, acostada y con el miembro inmóvil**.
- Retire anillos, pulseras y calzado (el miembro puede hincharse).
- Lave el lugar con agua y jabón.
- Llévela con urgencia a un hospital de referencia: **el suero antiofídico (antiveneno) es el único tratamiento eficaz**.
- Ofrezca agua si está consciente.

**NO haga:** torniquete o ligadura, cortes, succión, quemar, aplicar hierbas, queroseno, alcohol, café molido ni ninguna sustancia en el lugar, ni dar bebidas alcohólicas.

> Fuente: Ministério da Saúde (Brasil) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar. https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

validation_inputs.draft:
**NO apliques un torniquete (ligadura apretada) sobre la mordedura.** Esto puede cortar la circulación, causar gangrena y llevar a la amputación del miembro [S5].

La acción correcta depende de si hay acceso inmediato a tratamiento antiofídico, pero nunca uses un torniquete arterial:

**Pasos inmediatos:**
1.  **Alejarse:** Aléjese de la serpiente; tome una foto a distancia para identificación futura [S1].
2.  **Inmovilizar:** Mantenga a la víctima tranquila, acostada y con el miembro mordido completamente inmóvil (sin caminar) [S1] [S2].
3.  **Retirar objetos:** Quite anillos, pulseras y calzado antes de que haya hinchazón [S1].
4.  **Lavar:** Lave suavemente la herida con agua y jabón si es posible [S3].
5.  **Traslado urgente:** Lleve a la víctima inmediatamente al hospital más cercano o busque transporte en camilla; el suero antiofídico es el único tratamiento eficaz [S1] [S2].

**Lo que NO debe hacer:**
*   No use torniquetes ni ligaduras apretadas (pueden causar daño irreversible) [S5].
*   No intente extraer el veneno con succión, cortes o quemaduras [S5].
*   No aplique hierbas, alcohol, café molido ni otras sustancias en la herida [S1] [S5].

**Sin respaldo de fuentes locales (Consideraciones generales):**
La evidencia científica indica que el uso de torniquetes es generalmente ineficaz y peligroso. En algunos casos específicos (como ciertas cobras), se ha estudiado el vendaje compresivo, pero dado que la especie es desconocida, aplicar presión excesiva sin conocimiento local puede empeorar el daño tisular si el veneno es necrótico. La prioridad universal es la inmovilización del miembro y el traslado rápido a un centro médico [S3] [S5].

**⚠️ Señales de alarma:**
*   Hinchazón rápida que se extiende desde la mordedura.
*   Dolor intenso o mareos.
*   Dificultad para respirar o tragar.
*   Debilidad muscular o visión borrosa.

**Búsqueda de ayuda profesional:**
Si la víctima presenta dificultad para respirar, confusión o pérdida de conciencia, busque atención médica de emergencia inmediatamente. Esto no reemplaza el consejo médico; el antiveneno debe administrarse por profesionales en un entorno controlado [S1].

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra la fuente completa abajo. Esta sección no está disponible o es demasiado larga para incluirla completa.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

validation_inputs.draft:
**NÃO.** Não aplique um torniquete apertado ou garrote acima da picada.

Aqui estão os motivos e o procedimento correto:

1.  **Risco de Amputação:** Torniquetes são geralmente ineficazes contra venenos de cobras (exceto em casos muito específicos e raros de cobra-coral nas Filipinas) [S5]. O uso indevido pode cortar a circulação sanguínea, causar necrose e levar à amputação do membro [S5].
2.  **Contenção Improva:** Para a maioria dos venenos no Brasil (como cascavéis), o torniquete não impede a disseminação sistêmica eficazmente e aumenta o dano local nos tecidos [S1].
3.  **Alternativa Segura:** Se houver orientação médica específica para compressão (raro em casos de espécie desconhecida sem instrução prévia), utilize uma **bandagem compressiva**, não um torniquete apertado [S5]. No entanto, a regra geral para espécies desconhecidas é priorizar o imobilização do membro sem cortar a circulação.

**O que fazer agora:**

1.  **Afaste-se da cobra** e tire uma foto dela de longe se possível (sem tentar capturar) [S1].
2.  **Mantenha a vítima calma, deitada e com o membro picado imóvel** para retardar a circulação do veneno [S1]. Use uma maca ou peça ajuda para carregar a pessoa; evite que ela caminhe [S2].
3.  **Remova objetos** como anéis, pulseiras e sapatos imediatamente, pois o membro pode inchar [S1].
4.  **Lave o local** com água e sabão (se houver confirmação de que a limpeza não atrapalha a identificação futura do veneno para antiveneno) [S3].
5.  **Leve com urgência para um hospital.** O soro antiveneno é o único tratamento eficaz confirmado [S1].
6.  **Não faça:** cortes, sucção (boca ou bomba), queimaduras, aplicação de ervas/querosene/álcool/pó de café, nem dê bebida alcoólica [S1].

**Sem apoio de fontes locais:**
Em casos de espécie desconhecida, a incerteza sobre o tipo de veneno torna as técnicas controversas ainda mais perigosas. A literatura médica indica que tentativas caseiras como torniquetes rígidos frequentemente resultam em danos maiores do que a picada original [S5]. O foco deve ser estritamente na imobilização e no transporte rápido para atendimento profissional.

> **Atenção:** Esta orientação não substitui o atendimento médico. Procure ajuda imediatamente.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

validation_inputs.draft:
**No debes apretar la zona con un torniquete ni aplicar ligaduras.** Esto puede cortar la circulación, causar gangrena y llevar a la amputación del miembro [S5]. El uso de torniquetes está generalmente desaconsejado debido a la falta de evidencia de eficacia y al alto riesgo de daño tisular severo [S5].

**Acciones inmediatas:**

1.  **Mantén a la víctima inmóvil:** Acústala inmediatamente en el suelo o acostada para reducir la circulación sanguínea y la propagación del veneno [S1].
2.  **Retira objetos restrictivos:** Quita anillos, pulseras y calzado antes de que el miembro se hinche [S1].
3.  **Lava suavemente:** Lave el área con agua y jabón si es posible, pero evita limpiar en exceso si existe riesgo de perder trazas de veneno para identificación (depende del protocolo local) [S3].
4.  **Traslado urgente:** Organiza el transporte más rápido a un hospital; idealmente usa una camilla o ayuda para que no camine [S2].
5.  **Identificación:** Si es seguro, toma una foto de la serpiente desde lejos sin intentar atraparla [S1].

**Sin respaldo de fuentes locales:**
El tratamiento definitivo es el antiofídico (suero), solo administrado en un hospital por personal médico calificado [S1]. El uso de vendajes compresivos depende estrictamente del tipo de veneno y las indicaciones locales; al no conocer la especie, se debe evitar la compresión fuerte. Vigila constantemente la respiración de la víctima mientras obtienes ayuda.

**Señales de alarma:**
Busca atención médica inmediata si notas: hinchazón rápida, dolor intenso que se extiende, dificultad para respirar, vómitos o mareos [S4].

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]
